name: de Sitter
description: The maximally symmetric vacuum solution with constant positive curvature, driven by a positive cosmological constant. It models an exponentially expanding empty universe and describes both inflation and the far future of our cosmos.
history: Two years after publishing the general theory, Albert Einstein added a term to his field equations in 1917, the cosmological constant $\Lambda$, in an attempt to hold the universe static against its own gravity [einstein1917]. He had a particular cosmos in mind: ordinary matter spread uniformly through a closed, spherical space, with $\Lambda$'s repulsion finely tuned to balance the pull of the dust on itself exactly, so that nothing moved for all time. Within months the Dutch astronomer Willem de Sitter found a second solution to the very same amended equations [desitter1917]. He kept the same $\Lambda$ and threw out the matter, and the empty world that remained was not static.¶Which side of the equation $\Lambda$ is written on, geometry or vacuum energy, is a convention and changes no physics. The two solutions differ in their matter content: Einstein's a balance of dust against $\Lambda$ on a knife edge, de Sitter's the empty limit where only $\Lambda$ remains. Arthur Eddington later summed up the pair: Einstein's was matter without motion, de Sitter's motion without matter [eddington1933]. Peter Phillips built his story "Manna", in Astounding Science Fiction of February 1949, on that emptiness: the ghosts of two medieval monks leave a physicist a de Sitter version of the Riemann-Christoffel tensor, and he has to work out how anything can exist in a universe with neither matter nor radiation [phillips1949manna].¶Einstein objected in print on 7 March 1918: until the opposite was proved, he wrote, de Sitter's solution must be taken to have a genuine singularity on the surface $r = \pi R/2$, and there could be no spacetime without the matter that generates it [einstein1918]. Felix Klein took up the dispute in Göttingen at the end of that year, wrote de Sitter's world as a pseudosphere, the equation of an ordinary sphere in five variables with one sign changed, and showed that the place where its time coordinate fails is no worse a singularity than the origin of polar coordinates in a plane [klein1918]. Klein added that Einstein himself had pointed out to him in correspondence that the bare existence of this solution refutes the principle of no spacetime without matter [klein1918].¶De Sitter wrote his solution in static coordinates, and in that form it looked like a strange, empty, eternal world. The strangeness turned out to be an artifact of the coordinates. In 1925 Georges Lemaître, and independently Howard Robertson three years later, showed that the de Sitter universe could be rewritten in coordinates that are spatially flat and homogeneous, with a scale factor growing exponentially in time [lemaitre1925, robertson1928]. When Edwin Hubble published his relation between the distances and velocities of the nebulae in 1929, he called its outstanding feature the possibility that it represents the de Sitter effect [hubble1929]. The empty world looked static only in de Sitter's coordinates; it expands forever, and at an accelerating rate.¶The steady state universe is this metric with matter in it: Hermann Bondi and Thomas Gold required in 1948 that the universe look the same at every time as well as from every place, which fixes its metric as de Sitter's in these expanding coordinates and requires matter to be created continuously, at most one particle of the mass of a proton per liter in a billion years [bondi1948]. Fred Hoyle reached the same metric that year, with a constant density of matter, from field equations to which he added a term for creation [hoyle1948]. The standard theory does as well, William McCrea showed in 1951, if space carries a uniform stress, the matter created being the mass equivalent of the work that stress does as the universe expands [mccrea1951].¶The accelerating expansion is why cosmologists still study de Sitter space. It is the unique maximally symmetric solution with positive $\Lambda$, and it sits at both ends of modern cosmology: as the nearly exponential expansion of the inflationary epoch, and as the attractor at late times toward which a universe like our own, dominated by dark energy, appears to be heading [misner1973, wald1984]. In Jonathan Lethem's novel As She Climbed Across the Table of 1997 a physicist opens a Farhi-Guth universe, a bubble of de Sitter space, and explains that to adhere it to the Schwarzschild space outside he had to develop a pair of anti-trapped surfaces in an asymptotically Minkowskian background [lethem1997table]. Gary Gibbons and Stephen Hawking showed in 1977 that an observer in de Sitter space has an event horizon whose area can be interpreted as entropy, and that a particle detector the observer carries registers thermal radiation coming apparently from that horizon [gibbons1977]. Robert Wald proved in 1983 that expanding homogeneous universes with a positive cosmological constant evolve exponentially toward the de Sitter solution, for every Bianchi type but IX, and for type IX when $\Lambda$ is large enough [wald1983]. Two teams measuring distant supernovae of type Ia, one with Adam Riess and one with Saul Perlmutter as first author, found in 1998 and 1999 that the expansion of our own universe is accelerating, with a positive cosmological constant [riess1998, perlmutter1999].

related.text: A black hole placed in de Sitter space, so that a static observer sits between two horizons. At $r_s = 0$ it is de Sitter space.

The homogeneous, isotropic universe with any matter in it. Georges Lemaître and Howard Robertson showed that de Sitter space is one, with flat space and a scale factor growing exponentially [lemaitre1925, robertson1928].
The same geometry with its curvature reversed in sign, the vacuum of a negative cosmological constant. Its infinity is timelike [hawking1973].
De Sitter space with its expansion switched off, $\Lambda \to 0$, where the cosmological horizon recedes to infinity.
Einstein's universe of the same year, dust in balance against $\Lambda$ [einstein1917]. De Sitter space maps conformally onto a strip of it, where its conformal diagram is drawn [hawking1973].
Another vacuum with a positive cosmological constant, the product of de Sitter space of two dimensions and a sphere of the same radius [ortaggio2002].

A black hole with de Sitter space at its centre. Inside its inner horizon Bardeen's metric approaches de Sitter's static patch, which keeps the centre regular, and in the limit $g \to \infty$ at fixed $r_s/g^3$ it is de Sitter's everywhere [ansoldi2008].

A black hole whose core is a ball of de Sitter space with $\Lambda = 3/\ell^2$ whatever the mass. In the limit $m \to \infty$ at fixed $\ell$ the whole metric is de Sitter's [hayward2006, frolov2016].
De Sitter space with a rotating black hole put in. With the mass taken out again, Carter's metric is de Sitter space in spheroidal coordinates [akcay2011].
De Sitter space with charged black holes in it, each with a charge equal to its mass, carried along by the expansion or the contraction [kastor1993].

Schwarzschild's star of uniform density. Pawel Mazur and Emil Mottola showed in 2015 that with its radius taken down to its Schwarzschild radius the inside is a static patch of de Sitter space, with pressure $-\rho c^2$ throughout [mazur2015].

The homogeneous universes that expand at different rates in different directions. With a positive cosmological constant the differences die away: Robert Wald proved in 1983 that every expanding Bianchi universe but some of type IX approaches de Sitter space exponentially [wald1983].

A domain wall is a de Sitter space of one dimension fewer. In the flat space on either side the wall is the hyperboloid $X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 = 1/k^2 + c^2T^2$, and the metric induced on it is de Sitter's in $2 + 1$ dimensions [ipser1984, caldwell1996].
De Sitter space with a bubble of lower vacuum energy growing in it, the way a false vacuum decays [coleman1980].

A universe of radiation that also contracts, bounces, and expands with no singularity, and keeps the strong energy condition that de Sitter's violates. It has no closed trapped surface, and its slices of constant time are open [senovilla1998, chinea1992].
A ball of de Sitter space inside a thin shell, with Schwarzschild's vacuum outside. The vacuum within pushes outward on the shell, and no horizon forms [mazur2004].

De Sitter's static metric with a black hole added and $\Lambda r^2/3$ replaced by a power of the radius, $(r_q/r)^{3w+1}$. At $w = -1$ and $r_s = 0$ it is de Sitter's, with $\Lambda = 3/r_q^2$ [kiselev2003].
Gravitational waves of type N that cross de Sitter space on fronts shaped as hemispheres. With the profile switched off the metric is de Sitter space [bicak1999, griffiths2004].
De Sitter space with an impulsive gravitational wave on one cosmological horizon, the field of two massless particles. Off that horizon it is de Sitter space [hotta1993].

Erwin Schrödinger's remedy of 1956 for observers whose horizons part them: every event of de Sitter space made one with the event opposite it on the hyperboloid. An observer then sees one event of every pair, and the space has no global direction of time [schrodinger1956, parikh2003].
De Sitter space sliced into tubes $\mathbb{R} \times S^2$ and filled with dust that differs from shell to shell, Ruban's T-model of 1969 [ruban1969].

De Sitter space in imaginary time is a 4-sphere, the simplest compact gravitational instanton. The complex projective plane and Page's space are two more with a positive cosmological constant [gibbonshawking1979, page2009].
De Sitter space with each event identified with its images under a boost. J. Richard Gott and Li-Xin Li proposed it in 1998 as a universe whose earliest stretch of time is a loop [gott1998].

A closed Friedmann universe with points of its space identified under a group of 120 rotations of the 3-sphere. With nothing in it but a positive cosmological constant it is de Sitter space so identified, and it never stops expanding.

coordinates.name: Static Spherical

parameters.description: Cosmological constant, $\Lambda > 0$, carrying an inverse length squared. The horizon sits at $r = \sqrt{3/\Lambda}$ and the expansion rate of the flat slicing is $H = c\sqrt{\Lambda/3}$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
coordinates.line_element: ds^2 = -\left(1 - \dfrac{\Lambda r^2}{3}\right)c^2 dt^2 + \dfrac{dr^2}{1 - \dfrac{\Lambda r^2}{3}} + r^2 d\Omega^2

coordinates.name: Flat Slicing

parameters.description: Hubble rate, $H = c\sqrt{\Lambda/3}$, so that $\dfrac{3H^2}{c^2} = \Lambda$ and the horizon radius of the static patch is $c/H$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ comoving lengths, and the Hubble rate $H$ in place of $\Lambda$, related by $3H^2/c^2 = \Lambda$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
